description: Ego-policy swap experiment over scenarios/benchmark -- four junction scenarios (red_light, right_turn and stop_sign on Town10HD_Opt, left_turn on Town05) and three highway scenarios on Town04. Each scenario is run twice: once as compiled (the ego driven by its behaviour-tree timeline) and once with the ego's actuation handed to the IDM policy through the --ego-policy entry point. Everything else about the scenario -- NPC timelines, events, monitors, spawn geometry -- is identical between the two arms.

idm_parameters.note: Library defaults, identical across all seven scenarios, so the arm differs only in the controller and not in per-scenario tuning.

scenarios.name: red_light
scenarios.intent: A vehicle running the crossing red T-bones the ego inside the junction.

scenarios.name: right_turn
scenarios.intent: A vehicle already on the lane the ego turns onto rear-ends it.

scenarios.name: left_turn
scenarios.intent: An oncoming vehicle strikes the ego mid unprotected-left-turn.

scenarios.name: stop_sign
scenarios.intent: The ego negotiates an unsignalised crossing by precedence and nothing is hit.

scenarios.name: lane_change
scenarios.intent: The ego changes into the one neighbouring lane that is occupied, after the vehicle ahead brakes hard.

scenarios.name: cut_in
scenarios.intent: A faster vehicle passes the ego, cuts in ~7 m ahead of it and slows; the ego runs into the back of it.

scenarios.name: overtake
scenarios.intent: The ego pulls out past a slow lorry into the oncoming lane and meets an oncoming car head-on.

report_title: Swapping the ego controller on the CARLA benchmark
group_note: The two families fail differently, and that is why they are reported apart. A junction scenario stages its conflict at a place the ego has to cross, so an ego that arrives late or slow misses the conflict entirely and is instead rear-ended by its own scripted follower -- drive() has no braking driver model. A highway scenario stages its conflict in the ego's own lane, so a slower ego still meets it; what changes is when, and whether the ego ends up the striker or the struck.
town_note: left_turn is the one junction scenario not on Town10HD_Opt. drive() re-projects the actor onto the nearest lane every tick rather than following the waypoint chain it was routed onto, so inside a junction it can be captured by an overlapping connector. Driving the controller out of all 40 junction approaches on Town10HD_Opt finds six that execute a ~90 degree left turn and none of them crosses an anti-parallel oncoming lane, so an unprotected left cannot be staged there at all without ram(). Town05 junction 2328 is a plain four-way that connects the left turn only from the innermost lane, which is exactly the rule the local simulator's grid town implements. See the header of scenarios/benchmark/left_turn.osc.
construct_vocabulary: These scenarios use only constructs the paper documents -- Table 2's capability checklist and Listings 1-3 of the hello_world case study. ram(target:) has been removed: it appears nowhere in the paper, and every adversarial outcome in the four junction scenarios previously depended on it. The striking vehicle now keeps executing drive() on its own lane at its own declared speed; drive() has no car-following, yielding or collision-avoidance term, so not changing what you are doing IS failing to give way. See PIPELINE_WALKTHROUGH.md, 'Construct provenance'.
impulse_note: Peak impulses for the junction scenarios are not comparable with the ram-based runs recorded before them. ram applied full throttle regardless of the declared speed and steered onto the ego, so removing it changes the impact energy in both directions: right_turn falls from ~18600 to ~5160 and left_turn from ~20200 to ~5040, while red_light RISES from ~5300 to ~12300 because the truck now puts its full declared speed into the ego's flank instead of bleeding it in a turn. collision_occurred and the intended partner are unchanged, and those are what expect_collision and intended_partner test.
